messages.author: c3fba61596f3d3b8
messages.subject: Estimates meaning when psi~date (occu() function)
parts:
Hello,

I have a theoretical question: I use occu() function applied to
reproduction. I explain. We conducted multivisit sampling at several
sites (n=393). For analyses, we considered only sites occupied
(presence observed at least at one of our 4 visits) and then we code
data as follow: 0-no reproduction, 1-reproduction. Then, psi
represents the probability of reproduction.

I model psi~date. This model gives me estimates for psi for each
sampling date (predict() function) but I want to understand what it
refers to. It is the probability “by day” of reproduction, right? In
this case, how to obtain an estimate for all the season (I think the
mean is not appropriate)?

We want to estimate reproduction throughout the sampling season (among
observed individuals, how many reach the brood stage?). If the occu()
function only give us an estimate by days, we think of using
simulations to estimate reproduction over all our sampling period.

I know my reflection may seem unclear and feel free to ask me for
details.

Aude C.

Hi Aude,

technically, your model is a simple logistic regression for which you can use glm(). However, conceptually, I am not sure I understand your study fully. Perhaps you should check the literature for "nest success models" (Mayfield, and later developments) ?

Kind regards -- Marc

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: Estimates meaning when psi~date (occu() function)
parts:
Aude,

The problem with your current model is that date is not a site-specific attribute, while psi is trying to estimate a site-specific probability (if there are covariates).  You could model detection as varying with date (p~date) if you think the detectability of reproduction changes with date.  But I'm not sure how date would affect the probability of reproduction at a site.

I would consider using a multi-state model.  It sounds like you have data for sites where the species was not observed.  So you should be able to model the probability of presence and the probability of reproduction, conditional on presence (sensu Nichols et al. 2007 Ecology).  Date could then potentially affect your probability of detecting reproduction (delta in the Nichols paper).  If you are content with simply modeling the probability of reproduction given observed presence (using only those sites with observed presence), then at a least an occupancy model will allow an estimate of detection probability.  But you've conditioned your inference on sites where the species was observed, and obviously observed presence does not always equal presence.

Like Marc said, if you are interested in estimating nest success then you should consider looking into models of daily survival rate (Dinsmore et al. 2002 and Stanley 2004).  Those models typically require more frequent visitations than occupancy models, if you want your survival estimates to have any precision.

-Dan

messages.author: 527e14923215b7e4
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] R&N occupancy model
parts:
Hi Pablo,

The latent variable is N(i), the abundance at site i. An estimator of abundance in the sampled area, N, is the sum of the estimates of N(i). Here's an example for computing this, based on the example for occuRN:

data(birds)
woodthrushUMF <- unmarkedFrameOccu(woodthrush.bin)
(fm.wood.rn <- occuRN(~ 1 ~ 1, woodthrushUMF, K=25))
# Empirical Bayes estimates of abundance at each site
re <- ranef(fm.wood.rn, K=25)
plot(re)
Ni.hat <- bup(re, "mode")
N.hat <- sum(Ni.hat)

Richard
